RESUMO

Os

transtornos

mentais

frequentemente

se

iniciam

na

adolescência

e

no

início

da

vida

adulta

e

são

caracterizados

por

sobreposição

de

sintomas,

comorbidade

e

progressão

gradual.

Essas

características

desafiam

estratégias

tradicionais

de

rastreamento

baseadas

em

instrumentos

específicos

para

cada

transtorno,

sobretudo

em

contextos

com

restrições

de

recursos,

nos

quais

são

necessárias

abordagens

eficientes

de

detecção

precoce.

Nesse

cenário,

instrumentos

multidimensionais

e

transdiagnósticos

podem

representar

uma

alternativa

pragmática

para

identificar

sofrimento

psíquico

e

organizar

o

cuidado

em

jovens.

Esta

tese

avaliou

o

desempenho

da

Escala

Transversal

de

Sintomas

de

Nível

1

do

DSM-5

(
DSM-5

Level

1

Cross-Cutting

Symptom

Measure
;

DSM-XC),

proposta

pela

American

Psychiatric

Association,

como

instrumento

de

rastreamento

dimensional

em

uma

amostra

populacional

de

adultos

jovens

da

Coorte

de

Nascimentos

de

Pelotas

de

1993.

Desenvolvido

com

base

no

modelo

de

revisão

de

sistemas

da

medicina,

o

instrumento

examina

domínios

psicopatológicos

relevantes

no

contexto

assistencial.

Contudo,

a

capacidade

de

seus

domínios

em

informar

a

probabilidade

de

diagnósticos

específicos,

tanto

na

triagem

inicial

quanto

entre

indivíduos

com

transtornos

mentais,

não

havia

sido

previamente

avaliada,

e

os

pontos

de

corte

propostos

não

haviam

sido

empiricamente

testados.

A

investigação

foi

organizada

em

três

estudos.

O

primeiro

examinou

se

os

domínios

da

DSM-XC

funcionam

como

indicadores

específicos

de

transtornos

e

avaliou

o

impacto

do

enquadramento

adverbial

na

acurácia

diagnóstica.

Os

resultados

indicaram

que

os

domínios

operam

como

indicadores

transdiagnósticos,

modificando

simultaneamente

a

probabilidade

de

múltiplos

transtornos

internalizantes.

A

formulação

baseada

em

frequência

apresentou

maior

especificidade

e

maiores

razões

de

verossimilhança

positivas

do

que

a

formulação

baseada

em

intensidade.

O

segundo

estudo

avaliou

a

capacidade

dos

domínios

da

DSM-XC

em

detectar

comorbidade

psiquiátrica.

Embora

os

pontos

de

corte

originais

tenham

se

mostrado

úteis

para

excluir

diagnósticos

adicionais,

sua

capacidade

de

confirmação

foi

limitada.

A

elevação

dos

pontos

de

corte

produziu

melhora

modesta

na

confirmação

de

depressão,

ansiedade

e

transtornos

por

uso

de

substâncias,

com

pequenas

mudanças

nas

probabilidades

pós-teste.

Escores

elevados

em

domínios

específicos

não

confirmam

comorbidades,

mas

sinalizam

a

necessidade

de

investigação

clínica

sistemática.

Em

contraste,

o

escore

total

demonstrou

utilidade

como

indicador

de

elevada

carga

sintomática

e

potencial

multimorbidade.

O

terceiro

estudo

examinou

se

perfis

sintomáticos

derivados

da

DSM-XC

eram

consistentes

com

um

modelo

transdiagnóstico

de

estadiamento

clínico

na

comunidade.

Padrões

em

transtornos

do

humor,

ansiedade

e

estresse

pós-traumático

convergiram

ao

longo

de

continuum

de

sintomatologia,

e,

correspondendo

a

gradientes

crescentes

de

impacto

em

desfechos

de

saúde

e

funcionamento.

Estágios

iniciais

associaram-se

a

riscos

cardiometabólicos

e

comportamentais,

enquanto

estágios

persistentes

ou

recorrentes

concentraram

maiores

níveis

de

suicidalidade

e

desvantagem

socioeconômica.

Em

conjunto,

os

achados

sustentam

a

DSM-XC

como

instrumento

de

rastreio

dimensional

capaz

de

captar

gradientes

clinicamente

relevantes

de

sofrimento

psíquico

em

jovens

e

orientar

a

investigação

diagnóstica

em

nível

populacional.

Estudos

futuros

devem

avaliar

se

instrumentos

breves

e

multidimensionais

podem

apoiar

a

alocação

de

cuidados

informada

por

estágios

em

contextos

clínicos

e

de

saúde

pública.

Palavras-chave:

Epidemiologia

psiquiátrica;

Infância

e

adolescência;

Acurácia

diagnóstica;

Estadiamento;

Triagem.

ABSTRACT

Mental

disorders

frequently

emerge

during

adolescence

and

early

adulthood

and

are

characterized

by

symptom

overlap,

comorbidity,

and

gradual

progression.

These

features

challenge

traditional

screening

strategies

based

on

disorder-specific

instruments,

particularly

in

resource-constrained

settings

where

efficient

early

detection

approaches

are

required.

In

this

context,

multidimensional

and

transdiagnostic

instruments

may

represent

a

pragmatic

alternative

for

identifying

psychological

distress

and

organizing

care

in

young

people.

This

thesis

evaluated

the

performance

of

the

DSM-5

Level

1

Cross-Cutting

Symptom

Measure

(DSM-XC),

proposed

by

the

American

Psychiatric

Association,

as

a

dimensional

screening

instrument

in

a

population-based

sample

of

young

adults

from

the

1993

Pelotas

Birth

Cohort.

Developed

based

on

the

medical

review

of

systems

model,

the

instrument

examines

psychopathological

domains

relevant

to

clinical

care.

However,

the

extent

to

which

its

domains

inform

the

probability

of

specific

diagnoses,

both

in

initial

screening

and

among

individuals

with

established

mental

disorders,

had

not

been

previously

evaluated,

and

the

proposed

cut-off

points

had

not

been

empirically

tested.

The

investigation

was

organized

into

three

studies.

The

first

examined

whether

DSM-XC

domains

function

as

disorder-specific

indicators

and

assessed

the

impact

of

adverbial

symptom

framing

on

diagnostic

accuracy.

Results

indicated

that

the

domains

operate

as

transdiagnostic

indicators,

simultaneously

modifying

the

probability

of

multiple

internalizing

disorders.

Frequency-based

item

formulation

showed

greater

specificity

and

higher

positive

likelihood

ratios

than

intensity-based

formulation.

The

second

study

evaluated

the

ability

of

DSM-XC

domains

to

detect

psychiatric

comorbidity.

Although

the

original

cut-off

points

were

useful

for

ruling

out

additional

diagnoses,

their

rule-in

capacity

was

limited.

Increasing

cut-off

thresholds

resulted

in

modest

improvement

in

confirming

depression,

anxiety,

and

substance

use

disorders,

with

only

small

changes

in

post-test

probabilities.

Elevated

scores

in

specific

domains

do

not

confirm

comorbidities

but

signal

the

need

for

systematic

clinical

investigation.

In

contrast,

the

total

DSM-XC

score

demonstrated

utility

as

an

indicator

of

elevated

symptom

burden

and

potential

multimorbidity.

The

third

study

examined

whether

DSM-XC–derived

symptom

profiles

were

consistent

with

a

transdiagnostic

clinical

staging

model

in

the

community.

Patterns

across

mood,

anxiety,

and

post-traumatic

stress

disorders

converged

along

a

symptom

continuum

corresponding

to

increasing

gradients

of

impact

on

health

and

functioning

outcomes.

Early

stages

were

associated

with

cardiometabolic

and

behavioral

risks,

whereas

persistent

or

recurrent

stages

concentrated

higher

levels

of

suicidality

and

socioeconomic

disadvantage.

Taken

together,

these

findings

support

the

DSM-XC

as

a

dimensional

screening

instrument

capable

of

capturing

clinically

meaningful

gradients

of

psychological

distress

in

youth

and

guiding

diagnostic

investigation

at

the

population

level.

Future

studies

should

assess

whether

brief,

multidimensional

instruments

can

support

stage-informed

care

allocation

in

clinical

and

public

health

settings.

Psychiatric

epidemiology,

Childhood

and

adolescence,

Diagnostic

accuracy,

Staging,

Screening.

INTRODUCTION

Mental

disorders

constitute

one

of

the

leading

contributors

to

health-related

burden

during

adolescence

and

young

adulthood.

Epidemiological

evidence

indicates

that

more

than

three-quarters

of

mental

disorders

diagnosed

in

adulthood

have

their

onset

before

the

age

of

25

years

(Solmi

et

al.

2022);

moreover,

across

the

life

course,

approximately

25%

of

all

years

lived

with

disability

(YLDs)

attributable

to

mental

disorders

accumulate

before

this

age

(Kieling

et

al.

2024).

As

a

result,

adolescence

and

young

adulthood

represent

a

critical

developmental

period

during

which

preventive

and

early-intervention

strategies

may

substantially

influence

long-term

clinical

outcomes

(Davey

and

McGorry

2019;

McGorry

et

al.

2024).

This

developmental

window

is

particularly

relevant

for

low-

and

middle-income

countries

(LMICs),

where

the

majority

of

the

global

youth

population

resides

(Kieling

et

al.

2022),

and

mental

health

care

systems

frequently

operate

under

substantial

resource

constraints

that

require

contextually

adapted

and

scalable

approaches

(Patel

et

al.

2013;

Rose-Clarke

et

al.

2024).

Extending

detection

efforts

to

community-based

samples

in

LMICs

therefore

requires

the

development

and

evaluation

of

brief,

freely

available

assessment

tools

capable

of

supporting

timely

identification

without

imposing

substantial

financial

or

administrative

burden

on

already

resource-constrained

systems

(Farber

et

al.

2023;

Kohrt

et

al.

2018).

Accumulating

evidence

in

mental

health

research

indicates

that

psychiatric

disorders

are

highly

interconnected,

with

direct

implications

for

screening

and

early-intervention

strategies.

Converging

findings

from

genetic

architecture

(Bourque

et

al.

2024;

Jami

et

al.

2022),

neural

correlates

(Vanes

and

Dolan

2021;

Xie

et

al.

2023),

and

latent

variable

models

(Eaton

et

al.

2023),

among

other

lines

of

inquiry,

suggest

that

the

boundaries

between

disorders

are

less

clear-cut

than

traditionally

assumed.

This

reconceptualization

has

been

captured

by

the

notion

of

transdiagnostic

psychiatry,

which

emphasizes

dimensions,

processes,

and

mechanisms

that

cut

across

or

move

beyond

traditional

diagnostic

boundaries

(Fusar
‐
Poli

et

al.

2019).

In

this

framework,

transdiagnostic

approaches

may

target

characteristics

shared

across

disorders

(e.g.,

cognitive

patterns)

or

those

extending

beyond

diagnostic

categories

altogether

(e.g.,

functional

impairment).

In

the

present

thesis,

the

term

“transdiagnostic”

is

used

in

an

operational

sense,

corresponding

to

an

across-diagnoses

approach.

That

is,

rather

than

proposing

novel

constructs

beyond

existing

diagnostic

systems

or

analysing

overarching

characteristics

of

mental

disorders

(e.g.,

suffering),

this

work

examines

whether

a

brief

symptom

checklist

nested

into

domains

function

as

non-specific

indicators

that

cut

across

multiple

disorders.

Accordingly,

the

focus

is

on

evaluating

the

extent

to

which

these

measures

present

shared

diagnostic

accuracy

and

clinical

utility

across

established

diagnostic

categories.

In

parallel,

substantial

evidence

indicates

that

clinical

presentations

are

dimensional

in

nature

(Fried

et

al.

2022;

Haslam

et

al.

2012;

Hyman

2021),

spanning

a

continuum

from

lower

to

higher

levels

of

severity

without

a

sharp

boundary

between

health

and

illness.

This

dimensional

view

contrasts

with

earlier

categorical

conceptions

of

mental

disorder

rooted

in

Kraepelinian

diagnostic

dichotomies.

In

this

context,

there

has

been

growing

interest

in

the

development

of

assessment

approaches

aligned

with

transdiagnostic

and

dimensional

models

of

psychopathology

(Eaton

et

al.

2023;

Forbes

et

al.

2016;

Kotov

and

et

al.

2017;

Narrow

et

al.

2013;

Shah

et

al.

2020),

and

several

dimensional,

measurement-based

frameworks

have

been

proposed

in

recent

years.

Notable

examples

include

the

DSM’s

dimensional

symptom

measures

(American

Psychiatric

Association

2022;

Oquendo

et

al.

2026),

self-report

measures

derived

from

the

Hierarchical

Taxonomy

of

Psychopathology

(HiTOP)

(Simms

et

al.

2023),

and

service-oriented

personalized

care

models

embedded

within

emerging

youth

mental

health

systems.

For

instance,

the

Australian

“Right

Care,

First

Time”

framework

(Hickie

et

al.

2019)

operationalizes

several

transdiagnostic

and

dimensional

principles

within

an

applied

model

of

youth

mental

health

service

delivery.

The

DSM-5

Level

1

Cross-Cutting

Symptom

Measure

(DSM-XC)

represents

a

prominent

illustration

of

these

transdiagnostic,

dimensional

assessment

approaches

and

is

supported

by

the

Common

Measures

in

Mental

Health

Science

Initiative

(CMMHSI)

(Farber

et

al.

2023).

As

part

of

the

Diagnostic

and

Statistical

Manual

of

Mental

Disorders
,

one

of

the

most

widely

adopted

classificatory

systems

in

psychiatric

diagnosis

and

epidemiology,

assessment

measures

introduced

within

this

manual

are

likely

to

influence

clinical

assessment

practices,

service

organization,

and

population-level

surveillance.

Unlike

traditional

screening

tools,

the

DSM-XC

is

designed

to

function

as

a

mental

health

“review

of

systems”,

enabling

systematic

assessment

across

13

psychopathological

domains,

including

depression,

anxiety,

substance

use,

and

psychosis

(American

Psychiatric

Association

2013).

Of

particular

relevance

to

LMICs,

the

DSM-XC

was

selected

within

the

CMMHSI

in

part

due

to

practical

implementation

considerations,

including

free

availability,

brevity,

feasibility

of

administration

and

interpretation,

prior

use

in

research

settings,

and

potential

relevance

across

diverse

mental

health

contexts.

These

characteristics

position

the

DSM-XC

as

a

potentially

scalable

standard

measure,

particularly

in

settings

where

cost

and

respondent

burden

may

limit

the

uptake

of

other

tools.

Given

its

intended

role

as

a

standardized

multidimensional

screener

within

routine

care

and

research

environments,

rigorous

empirical

evaluation

of

its

measurement

properties

is

essential

to

ensure

that

its

implementation

meaningfully

improves

early

identification

and

clinical

decision-making

in

youth

mental

health

contexts.

The

DSM-XC

was

conceptualized

and

developed

by

the

DSM-5

Task

Force

and

Work

Groups

(Clarke

and

Kuhl

2014)

to

address

the

limitations

of

strict

categorical

diagnostic

systems

by

capturing

cross-cutting

symptomatology

commonly

observed

in

clinical

practice.

It

was

designed

to

be

administered

prior

to

clinical

evaluation

to

inform

decision-making,

rather

than

acting

as

a

standalone

diagnostic

screener.

Many

of

its

Level

1

items

were

derived

from

established

instruments,

such

as

the

Patient

Health

Questionnaire-2

(PHQ-2)

for

depression.

Early

feasibility

and

clinical

utility

were

established

during

the

large-scale

DSM-5

field

trials,

which

utilized

web-based

electronic

data

capture

across

diverse

adult

and

pediatric

academic

clinical

settings

in

the

United

States

and

Canada

(Clarke

et

al.

2013).

During

these

trials,

both

patients

and

clinicians

reported

that

the

measure

was

simple,

easy

to

use,

and

clinically

meaningful

(Mościcki

et

al.

2013).

Initial

psychometric

evaluations

within

these

trials

demonstrated

mostly

good-to-excellent

test-retest

reliability

coefficients

among

2,246

adult

patients

presenting

to

these

academic

clinics

with

various

existing

mental

health

diagnoses

(Narrow

et

al.

2013).

However,

the

measure

was

published

in

the

manual

and

recommended

for

routine

practice

based

primarily

on

these

reliability

metrics,

without

any

formal

validation

studies

having

been

carried

out

to

estimate

internal

consistency,

dimensionality,

predictive

value,

or

criterion

validity

against

gold-standard

diagnostic

interviews.

Despite

its

clinical

availability,

subsequent

independent

efforts

to

validate

the

DSM-XC

have

largely

relied

on

convenience

samples

and

comparisons

with

other

self-report

scales

rather

than

clinical

diagnoses.

For

example,

investigations

into

its

construct

validity

among

a

convenience

sample

of

non-treatment-seeking

college

students

supported

both

its

convergent

and

divergent

validity

(Bravo

et

al.

2018);

however,

this

was

demonstrated

solely

through

correlations

with

other

self-report

measures,

such

as

comparing

the

DSM-XC

Depression

domain

with

the

21-item

Depression

Anxiety

Stress

Scales

(DASS-21)

and

the

Substance

Use

domain

with

the

10-item

Alcohol

Use

Disorder

Identification

Test

(AUDIT).

Similarly,

the

largest

factor

analytic

study

to

date

(Gibbons

et

al.

2022)

sought

to

clarify

the

instrument's

underlying

dimensionality

using

an

online

convenience

sample

of

3,533

adults

(mean

age

46.5

±

14.8

years)

recruited

during

the

COVID-19

pandemic.

While

this

sample

was

not

fully

representative

of

the

general

population,

comprising

predominantly

white

(90.2%),

female

(83.2%),

and

highly

educated

(52.3%

with

advanced

degrees)

individuals,

the

confirmatory

factor

analysis

indicated

that

a

six-factor

model

(mood,

worry,

activation,

somatic

symptoms,

thought

content,

and

substance

use)

and

a

bifactor

solution

(a

general

psychopathology

factor

alongside

mood

and

anxiety

residuals)

fit

the

data

well.


Studies

attempting

to

assess

the

DSM-XC's

actual

screening

capabilities

have

similarly

suffered

from

significant

methodological

and

sampling

limitations.

The

measure

has

demonstrated

varying

degrees

of

sensitivity

and

specificity,

generally

showing

acceptable

sensitivity

but

poor

specificity,

when

applied

to

a

highly

morbid

clinical

population

of

inpatients

and

outpatients

with

substance

use

disorders

at

a

correctional

facility

(Bastiaens

and

Galus

2018).

Other

studies

evaluating

its

screening

utility

have

utilized

internet

convenience

samples

(Doss

and

Lowmaster

2022)

or

screened

healthy

research

volunteers

via

online

portals

(Mahoney

et

al.

2020),

comparing

DSM-XC

flags

against

clinical

triage

decisions

rather

than

comprehensive

diagnostic

evaluations.

While

these

previous

studies

suggest

the

DSM-XC

can

capture

relevant

psychopathological

variance,

their

reliance

on

scale-to-scale

correlations,

convenience

samples,

or

basic

triage

decisions

fails

to

provide

a

robust

diagnostic

validation.

Consequently,

there

remains

a

critical

lack

of

large-scale,

population-based

studies

that

rigorously

validate

the

DSM-XC

against

gold-standard

structured

clinical

interviews

across

multiple

diagnoses

to

determine

its

true

practical

utility

in

the

community.

Despite

its

increasing

adoption

in

clinical

and

research

settings,

comprehensive

cultural

adaptations

and

translations

of

the

DSM-XC

remain

limited.

While

a

few

studies

have

utilized

translated

versions,

such

as

Turkish

(Çökmüş

et

al.

2017),

Hindi

(Goel

and

Kataria

2018),

and

Urdu

(Ishfaq

and

Kamal

2019),

the

potential

biases

introduced

during

the

translation

process

and

the

cross-cultural

equivalence

of

the

measure's

dimensional

constructs

are

often

underexplored.

In

Brazil,

rigorous

evaluations

of

the

instrument's

semantic

and

cultural

adaptation

have

been

similarly

scarce,

raising

questions

about

how

well

the

measure's

items

capture

the

nuanced

expressions

of

psychological

distress

in

the

local

context.

For

the

present

work,

a

Brazilian

Portuguese

adaptation

of

the

DSM-XC

was

employed.

As

detailed

in

the

subsequent

chapters,

this

version

included

specific

modifications,

such

as

the

separation

of

double-barreled

questions

into

distinct

intensity

and

frequency

scales,

to

better

suit

the

cognitive

demands

of

the

community-based

youth

sample

(the

full

Portuguese

instrument

used

is

provided

in

the

Appendix).

Despite

its

promise,

several

methodological

issues

remain

insufficiently

examined

in

the

application

of

the

DSM-XC

specifically

and

of

brief

mental

health

screening

tools

for

youth

more

broadly.

In

particular,

key

assumptions

underlying

current

screening

paradigms,

including

the

disorder-specific

functioning

of

symptom

assessment

measures,

the

impact

of

adverbial

framing

on

symptom

reporting

(e.g.,

whether

symptoms

are

rated

based

on

frequency,

such

as

“how

often”,

or

intensity,

such

as

“how

much”),

the

capacity

of

measures

to

detect

psychiatric

comorbidity,

and

their

potential

role

in

operationalizing

transdiagnostic

clinical

staging,

have

rarely

been

evaluated

within

population-based

samples.

These

limitations

may

constrain

the

utility

of

multidimensional

tools

for

timely

identification

and

highlight

the

need

for

empirical

investigation

into

how

brief

cross-cutting

measures

perform

beyond

single-disorder

detection.

This

thesis

examines

these

challenges

from

the

perspective

of

the

performance

of

the

DSM-XC,

focusing

on

whether

this

tool

operates

as

intended

(i.e.,

multidimensionally)

across

key

measurement

properties

relevant

to

screening.

The

empirical

work

is

presented

in

three

papers:

the

first

addresses

assumptions

related

to

disorder-specific

functioning

and

adverbial

framing,

the

second

examines

its

capacity

to

detect

psychiatric

comorbidity,

and

the

third

explores

its

potential

role

in

informing

transdiagnostic

clinical

staging.

These

aspects

are

described

in

greater

detail

in

the

sections

below.

1.1

Gap

1:

Assumption

of

disorder

specificity

Despite

growing

interest

in

transdiagnostic

and

dimensional

approaches,

many

brief

screening

tools

are

developed

and

interpreted

based

on

the

assumption

of

disorder-specific

functioning,

a

premise

that

remains

largely

unexamined

empirically.

Recognizing

the

importance

of

early

identification,

major

expert

panels

such

as

the

U.S.

Preventive

Services

Task

Force

(USPSTF)

recommend

systematic

screening

for

conditions

like

anxiety,

depression,

and

suicide

risk

in

primary

care

settings

among

adolescents

and

young

adults

(US

Preventive

Services

Task

Force

et

al.

2023b;

US

Preventive

Services

Task

Force

et

al.

2023a).

However,

these

guidelines

focus

heavily

on

discrete

diagnostic

categories,

with

separate

tools

employed

to

screen

for

different

disorders.

Widely

used

assessment

measures

such

as

the

Patient

Health

Questionnaire-9

(PHQ-9)

(Kroenke

et

al.

2001)

for

depression

and

the

Generalized

Anxiety

Disorder-7

(GAD-7)

(Spitzer

et

al.

2006)

for

anxiety

further

exemplify

this

approach,

demonstrating

robust

diagnostic

accuracy

for

their

respective

target

conditions

(Negeri

et

al.

2021;

Plummer

et

al.

2016),

but

are

rarely

investigated

in

detection

of

closely

related

internalizing

disorders.

In

fact,

empirical

evidence

shows

that

these

tools

are

not

specific

for

detecting

their

intended

diagnostic

targets

(Jobim

et

al.

2025).

This

practice

rests

on

the

assumption

that

a

single

assessment

measure

should

map

exclusively

to

a

single

mental

health

condition.

While

operationally

convenient,

this

assumption

contrasts

with

the

typical

presentation

of

mental

health

symptoms

in

clinical

practice,

where

comorbidity

and

shared

etiological

factors

are

the

norm

rather

than

the

exception

(Krueger

and

Eaton

2015;

McGrath

et

al.

2020;

Plana-Ripoll

et

al.

2019).

Furthermore,

recent

empirical

work

highlights

that

symptoms

such

as

insomnia

and

irritability

often

overlap

across

diagnostic

criteria

(Forbes

et

al.

2024),

challenging

the

current

practice

of

assessing

disorders

in

isolation.

Despite

the

prevalence

of

disorder-specific

screening

recommendations,

diagnostic

accuracy

research

has

rarely

evaluated

multiple

mental

health

conditions

simultaneously

to

test

the

potential

limitations

of

this

approach

(Caspi

et

al.

2025;

Jobim

et

al.

2025;

Kohrt

et

al.

2025).


Although

the

DSM-XC

utilizes

a

dimensional

assessment

structure

to

capture

symptom

severity,

it

retains

a

pragmatic

link

to

traditional

diagnostic

categories

through

a

two-tiered

process.

A

positive

result

on

the

Level

1

screener,

defined

by

specific

thresholds

for

each

domain,

acts

as

a

trigger

for

a

more

detailed

Level

2

domain-specific

assessment

(American

Psychiatric

Association

2013).

1.2

Gap

2:

Influence

of

symptom

framing

Despite

the

potential

of

the

DSM-XC

as

a

comprehensive

screening

tool,

critical

methodological

issues

remain

regarding

its

original

operationalization.

The

assessment

measure

employs

a

double-barreled

question

structure,

asking

respondents

“how

much

(or

how

often)”

they

have

been

bothered

by

a

symptom

over

the

past

two

weeks.

This

combined

phrasing

forces

patients

to

simultaneously

evaluate

and

integrate

two

distinct

aspects

of

their

experience,

severity

(intensity)

and

duration

or

recurrence

(frequency),

into

a

single

response.

Evidence

from

pilot

testing

in

the

Pelotas

Birth

Cohort

has

indicated

that

this

ambiguity

creates

cognitive

demand

and

confusion,

as

participants

struggle

to

interpret

the

combined

prompt,

potentially

compromising

the

clarity

and

accuracy

of

the

assessment.

The

impact

of

such

framing

choices

is

not

merely

semantic;

methodological

research

suggests

that

asking

about

intensity

versus

frequency

can

elicit

significantly

different

response

patterns

and

psychometric

properties

(Gong

et

al.

2013;

Levin

et

al.

1998).

For

instance,

frequency-based

ratings

have

been

associated

with

higher

reliability,

criterion

validity

(Krishnakumar

et

al.

2021),

and

stability

over

time

(Krabbe

and

Forkmann

2014)

when

compared

to

intensity

ratings,

which

may

be

more

susceptible

to

subjective

interpretation.

Furthermore,

the

lack

of

standardization

in

adverbial

framing

contributes

to

substantial

heterogeneity

in

mental

health

assessment,

undermining

the

comparability

of

data

across

studies

and

clinical

settings

(Newson

et

al.

2020).

Despite

these

methodological

concerns,

the

relative

diagnostic

accuracy

of

these

distinct

framings

has

not

been

systematically

evaluated

within

the

context

of

the

DSM-XC.

It

remains

unclear

whether

separating

these

dimensions,

specifically,

asking

“how

often”

versus

“how

much”,

would

improve

the

measure's

ability

to

detect

mental

disorders

or

rule

them

out.

Determining

which

framing

provides

superior

screening

utility

is

therefore

essential,

not

only

for

optimizing

the

diagnostic

performance

of

the

DSM-XC

but

also

for

establishing

clearer

standards

for

the

future

development

of

psychiatric

assessment

measures.

1.3

Gap

3:

Detection

of

psychiatric

comorbidity

Beyond

understanding

the

impact

of

adverbial

framing,

the

capacity

of

screening

tools

to

accurately

detect

psychiatric

comorbidity

remains

a

significant

clinical

gap.

Psychiatric

comorbidity

is

consistently

associated

with

poorer

long-term

outcomes,

including

elevated

risk

of

chronic

physical

illness

(Scott

et

al.

2016),

higher

healthcare

costs

(Christensen

et

al.

2023),

and

reduced

life

expectancy

(Plana
‐
Ripoll

et

al.

2020).

Moreover,

compared

with

individuals

whose

disorders

first

emerge

later

in

life,

those

with

early-onset

conditions

demonstrate

a

more

rapid

accumulation

of

additional

psychiatric

diagnoses

over

time,

(McGrath

et

al.

2020)

underscoring

the

importance

of

early,

comprehensive

assessment

strategies.


Despite

these

consequences,

comorbidity

is

frequently

under-recognized

in

routine

clinical

settings,

particularly

when

clinicians

rely

on

unstructured

interviews

rather

than

structured

assessments

(Zimmerman

and

Mattia

1999).

In

the

context

of

time-constrained

practice,

clinicians

may

prioritize

the

first

diagnosed

condition

or

the

“chief

complaint”,

often

limiting

further

investigation

into

additional

disorders.

While

structured

interviews

could

mitigate

this

oversight,

they

are

typically

too

time-consuming

for

routine

use

in

clinical

settings.

Consequently,

brief

screening

tools

are

essential

to

support

the

systematic

early

detection

of

multimorbidity

and

ensure

that

complex

clinical

presentations

are

not

overlooked

(Arrarás

et

al.

2023).

However,

empirical

work

on

screening

tools

designed

specifically

to

detect

comorbidity

is

limited.

Most

existing

research

is

derived

from

the

Psychiatric

Diagnostic

Screening

Questionnaire

(PDSQ),

which

was

validated

primarily

in

adults

and

may

not

generalize

well

to

youth

or

early-intervention

contexts

(Zimmerman

and

Chelminski

2006;

Zimmerman

and

Mattia

2001).

Although

the

DSM-XC

was

explicitly

developed

to

assist

clinicians

in

identifying

comorbidities

that

could

impact

treatment

and

prognosis

(American

Psychiatric

Association

2013),

its

actual

diagnostic

performance

in

detecting

secondary

disorders

among

individuals

who

already

have

a

primary

diagnosis

has

not

been

empirically

tested.

Consequently,

there

is

a

significant

gap

in

understanding

how

brief

screeners

perform

in

the

context

of

multimorbidity.

Establishing

the

ability

of

the

DSM-XC

to

effectively

rule

out

or

confirm

additional

diagnoses

is

therefore

important

to

support

its

use

as

a

comprehensive

tool

for

comorbidity

assessment.

1.4

Gap

4:

Internal

coherence

of

clinical

staging

Finally,

the

dimensional

structure

of

the

DSM-XC

offers

a

standardized

metric

to

evaluate

the

coherence

of

transdiagnostic

staging

frameworks.

Clinical

staging

conceptualizes

mental

disorders

not

as

static

categories,

but

as

dynamic

processes

progressing

along

a

continuum

of

severity,

ranging

from

asymptomatic

states

(Stage

0)

and

non-specific

distress

(Stage

1a)

to

subthreshold

phenotypes

(Stage

1b)

and

established

or

persistent

illness

(Stages

2

to

4).

The

utility

of

this

approach

has

increasingly

extended

beyond

conceptual

models

into

service

delivery,

informing

the

redesign

of

youth

mental

health

systems.

A

prominent

example

is

the

“Right

Care,

First

Time”

model

(Hickie

et

al.

2019),

which

explicitly

integrates

clinical

staging

with

multidimensional

assessment

to

guide

early

intervention.

However,

such

staging

models

have

been

primarily

developed

and

implemented

in

help-seeking

cohorts

within

specialized

services

in

high-income

countries.

Although

these

clinical

settings

are

appropriate

for

evaluating

service-level

applications

of

staging,

they

tend

to

include

individuals

who

are

already

experiencing

more

severe

or

impairing

forms

of

illness.

In

community

populations,

particularly

in

low-

and

middle-income

countries,

mental

health

symptoms

often

emerge

outside

formal

care

pathways,

and

individuals

at

earlier

stages

are

less

likely

to

be

identified

through

service-based

sampling.

As

a

result,

whether

staging

frameworks

retain

their

construct

validity

(Clarke

et

al.

2025)

when

applied

beyond

clinical

samples

remains

uncertain.

This

limitation

is

compounded

by

the

absence

of

a

standardized

approach

for

operationalizing

clinical

stages

in

population-based

settings.

A

brief,

targeted

literature

review

conducted

for

this

thesis

identified

substantial

heterogeneity

in

how

stages

are

defined

across

disorders,

instruments,

and

thresholds,

with

most

community-based

applications

focusing

on

specific

transitions

between

stages

or

on

longitudinal

progression

across

symptom

domains.

Only

a

small

number

of

empirical

studies

(Chen

et

al.

2025;

Ratheesh

et

al.

2025;

Ratheesh

et

al.

2023)

have

attempted

to

operationalize

transdiagnostic

staging

models

in

longitudinal

community

cohorts.

In

the

absence

of

a

gold-standard

framework

for

defining

stages

across

mood,

anxiety,

and

stress-related

disorders

in

community

samples,

the

staging

model

employed

in

the

third

study

of

this

thesis

was

developed

following

a

review

of

the

available

literature

and

recent

advances

in

public

mental

health

staging

(Buchweitz

et

al.

2026;

Chen

et

al.

2025;

Dwyer

et

al.

2025;

Haas

et

al.

2025;

Scott

et

al.

2024).

Based

on

this

review,

an

expert

panel

composed

of

four

psychiatrists,

including

two

with

prior

research

experience

in

clinical

staging

models,

reached

consensus

on

operational

criteria

integrating

symptom

presence,

diagnostic

status,

impairment,

and

chronicity

for

each

disorder

category.

In

this

context,

stage-specific

symptom

profiles

were

examined

among

individuals

classified

within

the

same

clinical

stage,

irrespective

of

their

primary

diagnosis.

These

profiles

were

defined

as

the

pattern

of

cross-cutting

symptoms

observed

via

the

DSM-XC

within

each

stage.

Specifically,

this

thesis

employs

the

DSM-XC

to

examine

whether

these

patterns

remain

consistent

across

different

diagnostic

categories

within

the

same

stage

(as

defined

by

structured

clinical

interviews),

thereby

testing

the

internal

coherence

of

the

transdiagnostic

model.


Furthermore,

this

framework

was

examined

to

determine

whether

successive

stages

correspond

to

objective

gradients

in

external

indicators

of

clinical

burden.

Specifically,

transdiagnostic

stages

were

compared

with

respect

to

the

prevalence

of

cardiometabolic

risk,

suicidal

ideation,

and

NEET

status

(not

in

education,

employment,

or

training),

in

order

to

assess

whether

stage

progression

is

associated

with

systematic

differences

in

physical

health

vulnerability

and

socio-occupational

disengagement.

1.5

Rationale

Four

critical

knowledge

gaps

drive

the

present

thesis,

highlighting

the

need

for

a

detailed

examination

of

the

properties

and

functions

of

brief

screeners

like

the

DSM-XC.

To

address

these

gaps

and

target

key

limitations

of

current

screening

paradigms,

the

present

analysis

adopts

a

clinimetric

(Fava

et

al.

2025)

rather

than

a

strictly

psychometric

approach.

This

framework

is

particularly

appropriate

because

the

DSM-XC

is

already

published

and

indicated

for

routine

clinical

use

from

the

DSM-5

onwards.

While

traditional

psychometric

evaluations

emphasize

the

homogeneity

of

scale

components

and

unidimensionality,

a

clinimetric

approach

is

designed

to

accommodate

the

heterogeneous

features

of

clinical

variables.

Consequently,

rather

than

focusing

on

internal

consistency

or

latent

factor

models,

this

thesis

evaluates

the

DSM-XC

based

on

its

discrimination

properties—specifically,

its

capacity

to

accurately

differentiate

among

distinct

clinical

subgroups.

By

examining

the

instrument's

ability

to

provide

a

broad

rating

of

clinical

phenomena,

this

research

investigates

its

practical

utility

for

determining

diagnostic

probability,

detecting

psychiatric

comorbidity,

and

characterizing

progressive

illness

staging

within

a

population-based

setting,

ultimately

aiming

to

support

clinical

judgment

and

decision-making

in

epidemiology

and

public

health.

First,

while

guidelines

prioritize

disorder-specific

screening,

it

remains

uncertain

whether

short

measures

operate

in

a

truly

disorder-specific

manner

or

if

they

function

transdiagnostically,

influencing

the

likelihood

of

multiple

disorders

simultaneously.


Second,

the

specific

diagnostic

impact

of

assessing

symptom

frequency

(“how

often”)

versus

intensity

(“how

much”)

remains

untested.

To

address

these

ambiguities,

the

first

study

assesses

the

screening

properties

of

the

DSM-XC

domains

for

eight

distinct

psychiatric

disorders,

directly

comparing

the

diagnostic

accuracy

of

intensity-based

versus

frequency-based

scoring.


Third,

despite

the

clinical

importance

of

identifying

multimorbidity,

the

accuracy

of

cross-cutting

measures

for

specifically

detecting

comorbid

psychiatric

disorders

among

youth

has

not

been

evaluated

against

optimized

thresholds.

To

bridge

this

gap,

the

second

study

evaluates

the

capacity

of

the

DSM-XC

to

identify

psychiatric

comorbidity

among

youth

with

a

primary

diagnosis,

testing

original

DSM-5

thresholds

against

optimized

cut-offs

derived

to

enhance

detection.

In

this

study,

we

adopted

a

disorder-specific

approach,

examining

seven

psychiatric

disorders

that

had

direct

correspondent

domains

within

the

DSM-XC

available

in

the

cohort’s

assessment

battery.

Finally,

while

clinical

staging

offers

a

promising

framework

for

tracking

illness

progression,

the

potential

of

dimensional

screeners

to

characterize

successive

transdiagnostic

stages

of

illness

severity

in

the

community

has

not

been

established.

Consequently,

the

third

study

assesses

a

transdiagnostic

clinical

staging

framework

encompassing

mood,

anxiety,

and

post-traumatic

stress

disorders,

verifying

if

the

DSM-XC

captures

coherent

cross-cutting

symptom

profiles

across

progressive

stages

and

quantifying

their

association

with

objective

indicators

of

health,

social,

and

functional

burden.

This

study

focused

exclusively

on

these

disorder

categories

because

they

represent

the

psychiatric

conditions

with

the

highest

health-related

burden

among

youth.

Collectively,

these

studies

examine

how

the

DSM-XC

performs

in

detecting

mental

disorders

and

for

characterizing

gradients

of

symptom

expression

across

successive

clinical

stages

among

youth

in

a

population-based

setting.

externalizing

disorders

(antisocial

personality,

attention-deficit/hyperactivity,

and

alcohol

use

disorders).

Sensitivities

and

specificities

>0.75,

LR+>2

and

LR-<0.5

were

considered

meaningful.

Values

were

calculated

for

the

DSM-XC’s

original

scoring

and

for

adverbial

framings.

Results.

Several

DSM-XC

domains

demonstrated

meaningful

screening

properties.

The

anxiety

domain

exhibited

acceptable

sensitivity

and

LR-

values

for

all

internalizing

disorders.

The

suicidal

ideation,

psychosis,

memory,

repetitive

thoughts

and

behaviours,

and

dissociation

domains

displayed

acceptable

specificity

for

all

disorders.

Domains

also

yielded

small

but

meaningful

LR+

values

for

internalizing

disorders.

However,

LR+

and

LR-

values

were

not

generally

meaningful

for

externalizing

disorders.

Frequency-framed

questions

improved

screening

properties.

Conclusions.

The

DSM-XC

domains

showed

transdiagnostic

screening

properties,

providing

small

but

meaningful

changes

in

the

likelihood

of

internalizing

disorders

in

the

community,

which

can

be

improved

by

asking

frequency

of

symptoms

compared

to

intensity.

The

DSM-XC

is

currently

lacking

meaningful

domains

for

externalizing

disorders.

Introduction

There

is

a

growing

clinical

and

academic

interest

in

investigating

symptoms

that

cut

across

multiple

mental

disorders

(Eaton

et

al.,

2023;

Forbes

et

al.,

2023;

Gibbons,

Farmer,

Shaw,

&

Chung,

2023),

such

as

anxiety,

insomnia,

depressed

mood,

hallucinations,

among

others.

Both

authoritative

texts

(American

Psychiatric

Association,

2013)

and

empirical

studies

(Forbes,

Tackett,

Markon,

&

Krueger,

2016;

Waszczuk

et

al.,

2017)

have

encouraged

dimensional

approaches

to

psychopathology

assessment,

with

the

aim

of

elucidating

shared

features

among

different

disorders.

An

emerging

tool

is

The

Diagnostic

and

Statistical

Manual

of

Mental

Disorders-5

(DSM-5)

Level

1

Cross-Cutting

Symptom

Measure

(DSM-XC),

which

consists

of

23

self-reported

questions

that

explore

13

different

mental

health

domains.

However,

the

current

body

of

evidence

supporting

the

utility

of

cross-cutting

symptom

assessments,

including

the

DSM-XC,

remains

limited.

This

gap

presents

an

unexplored

opportunity

not

only

for

understanding

the

connections

between

different

diagnostic

categories

but

also

for

optimizing

community-based

mental

disorder

screening.

The

U.S.

Preventive

Services

Task

Force

(USPSTF)

supports

the

use

of

disorder-specific

scales

in

screening

recommendations

for

anxiety

(US

Preventive

Services

Task

Force

et

al.,

2023a),

depression

(US

Preventive

Services

Task

Force

et

al.,

2023b),

and

unhealthy

drug

and

alcohol

use

among

adults

(US

Preventive

Services

Task

Force

et

al.,

2020;

US

Preventive

Services

Task

Force

et

al.,

2018).

Notable

scales

presenting

good

diagnostic

accuracy

for

these

purposes

(Mulvaney-Day

et

al.,

2018)

include

the

Patient

Health

Questionnaire-9

(PHQ-9,

sensitivity=0.85,

specificity=0.85)

and

Center

for

Epidemiological

Studies

Depression

(CES-D,

sensitivity=0.83,

specificity=0.78)

for

major

depression

(Negeri

et

al.,

2021;

Vilagut,

Forero,

Barbaglia,

&

Alonso,

2016),

the

General

Anxiety

Disorder-7

(GAD-7)

for

generalized

anxiety

disorder

(sensitivity=0.83,

specificity=0.84)

(Plummer,

Manea,

Trepel,

&

McMillan,

2016),

the

National

Institute

on

Alcohol

Abuse

and

Alcoholism

(NIAAA)

for

current

alcohol

use

disorder

(sensitivity=0.88,

specificity=0.67)

(Smith,

Schmidt,

Allensworth-Davies,

&

Saitz,

2009),

The

Alcohol,

Smoking

and

Substance

Involvement

Screening

Test

(ASSIST)

for

tobacco,

alcohol,

and

cannabis

use

disorders

(sensitivities=0.95-1.00;

specificities=0.79-0.93)

(Gryczynski

et

al.,

2015),

and

the

Tobacco,

Alcohol,

Prescription

Medication

and

Other

Substance

Use

(TAPS,

sensitivities=0.70-0.74,

specificities

0.85-0.95

for

tobacco,

alcohol

and

marijuana)

(McNeely

et

al.,

2016),

among

others.

Nevertheless,

current

recommendations

lack

the

inclusion

of

multi-disorder

tools.

Only

a

handful

of

such

screening

instruments

are

available,

such

as

the

PHQ-4,

The

Hospital

Anxiety

and

Depression

Scale

(HADS),

and

the

Mental

Health

Index

(MHI-5).

The

PHQ-4

(Löwe

et

al.,

2010)

is

an

ultra-short

assessment

that

combines

the

PHQ-2

(sensitivity

=

0.89,

specificity

=

0.75)

(Mitchell,

Yadegarfar,

Gill,

&

Stubbs,

2016)

and

GAD-2

(sensitivity

=

0.80,

specificity

=

0.81)

(Plummer

et

al.,

2016),

facilitating

simultaneous

screening

for

depression

and

anxiety.

The

HADS

is

a

lengthier

but

commonly

used

tool

for

identifying

depression

and

anxiety

in

medically

ill

patients,

with

sensitivities

and

specificities

for

depression

and

anxiety

subscales

of

approximately

0.80

(Bjelland,

Dahl,

Haug,

&

Neckelmann,

2002).

However,

the

extent

of

diagnostic

insight

provided

by

comprehensive

assessments

remains

largely

unexplored

for

psychiatric

disorders.

The

symptoms

included

in

the

DSM-XC

exhibit

similarities

to

the

PHQ-2

(Löwe,

Kroenke,

&

Gräfe,

2005;

Mitchell

et

al.,

2016)

and

the

GAD-2

(Plummer

et

al.,

2016).

However,

the

utility

of

these

scales

has

been

ascertained

only

for

the

specific

diagnoses

they

were

designed

to

screen

for.

Given

the

recognized

high

comorbidity

among

mental

disorders

(Plana-Ripoll

et

al.,

2019)

and

the

occurrence

of

overlapping

symptoms

across

diagnoses

(Forbes

et

al.,

2023),

it

is

pertinent

to

consider

expanding

the

use

of

these

brief

screeners

to

identify

multiple

disorders.

In

addition,

a

comprehensive

examination

of

the

screening

properties

of

the

13

DSM-XC

domains

can

help

pinpoint

which

cross-cutting

symptoms

are

more

effective

in

either

confirming

or

ruling

out

specific

diagnoses.


Previous

studies

suggested

the

DSM-XC

(Bastiaens

&

Galus,

2018;

Doss

&

Lowmaster,

2022;

Mahoney

et

al.,

2020)

could

be

used

for

screening,

but

they

lacked

the

use

of

diagnostic

interviews

and

assessed

convenience

samples

with

limited

generalizability

and

ecological

validity.

Additionally,

the

DSM-XC

merges

questioning

about

the

intensity

(“how

much”)

and

frequency

(“how

often”)

of

symptoms,

which

could

impact

its

psychometric

and

screening

properties

(Gong

et

al.,

2013;

Krabbe

&

Forkmann,

2014;

Krishnakumar

et

al.,

2021;

Levin,

Schneider,

&

Gaeth,

1998),

but

empirical

studies

on

the

impact

on

screening

utility

of

different

framings

is

not

known.

Our

aim

was

to

assess

the

screening

properties

(sensitivity,

specificity,

and

likelihood

ratios

[LRs])

of

the

DSM-XC’s

domains

to

detect

8

mental

disorders,

representative

of

both

internalizing

and

externalizing

spectra,

in

the

community.

We

will

address

this

by

assessing

the

instruments’

original

operationalization

merging

intensity

and

frequency

of

symptoms

and

conduct

an

analysis

for

both

framings

separately.

The

DSM-5

Level

1

Cross-Cutting

Symptom

Measure


The

DSM-XC

is

a

self-reported

measure

that

examines

different

mental

health

domains

to

assist

clinicians

in

identifying

comorbidity

that

could

impact

a

patient's

treatment

and

prognosis

(American

Psychiatric

Association,

2013).

The

cross-cutting

measures

for

adults

involve

two

levels

of

inquiry.

At

Level

1,

the

questionnaire

consists

of

23

items

distributed

in

13

domains:

depression,

anger,

mania,

anxiety,

somatic

symptoms,

suicidal

ideation,

psychosis,

sleep

problems,

memory,

repetitive

thoughts

and

behaviours,

dissociation,

personality

functioning,

and

substance

use.

Items

ask,

“how

much

(or

how

often)

have

you

been

bothered

by”

a

given

problem

during

the

previous

two

weeks

and

provide

a

5-point

Likert

scale

ranging

from

0

=

“None

(not

at

all)”

to

4

=

“Severe

(nearly

every

day)”.

A

rating

of

mild

(i.e.,

2)

or

greater

on

any

item

within

a

domain,

except

for

substance

use,

suicidal

ideation,

and

psychosis

is

considered

a

positive

screen.

For

substance

use,

suicidal

ideation,

and

psychosis,

a

rating

of

slight

(i.e.,

1)

or

greater

on

any

item

within

the

domain

is

considered

a

positive

domain.

The

threshold

scores

in

any

of

its

domains

indicate

the

need

for

a

thorough

clinical

investigation

with

the

respective

Level

2

Cross-Cutting

Symptom

Measure.

Level

2

questions

offer

a

more

detailed

assessment

of

specific

domains.

Except

for

suicidal

ideation,

psychosis,

memory

problems,

dissociation

and

personality

functioning,

each

domain

in

the

adult

version

of

the

DSM-XC

corresponds

to

a

Level

2

measure,

which

contains

more

questions

about

each

screened

disorder.

Additional

details

on

Level

1

and

Level

2

measures

can

be

found

online

at

www.psychiatry.org/dsm5.

In

the

original

DSM-XC,

there

are

two

simultaneous

framings

when

asking

about

symptoms:

intensity

(i.e.,

how

much)

and

frequency

(i.e.,

how

often),

requiring

the

respondent

to

choose

a

single

answer.

After

a

pilot

test

in

Brazil,

we

identified

that

some

participants

had

difficulty

understanding

the

double-barrelled

questions,

which

led

to

the

decision

to

split

each

question

into

two,

and

answers

were

recorded

on

two

separate

5-point

scales:

one

for

intensity

and

another

for

frequency.

To

compute

the

score

as

intended

by

the

original

DSM-XC

“OR”

rule,

the

highest

score

in

each

question

was

considered

when

analysed

jointly.

For

example,

an

answer

of

0

(none)

for

how

much

and

2

(several

days)

for

how

often,

or

vice

versa,

was

coded

as

2.

An

additional

adaptation

was

made

to

the

instrument

by

dividing

the

last

item

(item

23)

into

two

(items

23

and

24,

as

shown

in

Supplementary

Table

1)

to

allow

for

the

exploration

of

substance

use

and

self-prescription/misuse

separately.

Assessment

of

psychiatric

diagnoses

Participants

were

also

assessed

for

the

presence

of

psychiatric

disorders

with

an

adapted

Brazilian

version

of

the

MINI

International

Neuropsychiatric

Interview

(MINI)

(Amorim,

2000),

administered

by

trained

clinical

psychologists,

who

did

not

have

access

to

the

DSM-XC

responses.

The

MINI

5.0.0

is

a

structured

and

standardized

diagnostic

interview

based

on

the

4th

edition

of

the

Diagnostic

and

Statistical

Manual

of

Mental

Disorders

(DSM-IV)

(American

Psychiatric

Association,

1994),

and

was

used

to

assess

the

following

disorders:

antisocial

personality

disorder

(APD),

attention-deficit/hyperactivity

disorder

(ADHD),

bipolar

disorder

(BD),

generalized

anxiety

disorder

(GAD),

major

depressive

disorder

(MDD),

stress

disorder

(PTSD)

social

anxiety

disorder

(SAD).

Moreover,

to

capture

the

DSM’s

impairment

criterion,

we

included

an

additional

question

participants

how

much

impairment

the

reported

symptoms

in

their

life,

mild,

moderate

or

severe

(Manfro

et

al.,

2021;

Matte

et

al.,

2015).

of

as

a

score

moderate

or

severe.

The

Alcohol

Use

Disorders

Identification

Test

(AUDIT),

a

10-question

instrument,

was

used

to

identify

participants

with

active

alcohol

use

disorder

(AUD).

A

score

of

≥

15

for

men

and

≥

13

for

women

was

considered

positive.

The

AUDIT

validity

has

been

previously

investigated

in

Brazil

(Meneses-Gaya

et

al.,

2010).

analyses

followed

the

Standards

for

Reporting

of

Diagnostic

Accuracy

Studies

(STARD)

guidelines

(Bossuyt

Screening

properties

We

estimated

the

number

of

true

positives,

false

positives,

true

negatives,

and

false

negatives

for

each

of

the

13

DSM-XC

domains

to

detect

individuals

with

psychiatric

disorders.

We

then

estimated

the

sensitivity,

specificity,

positive

(LR+)

and

negative

(LR-)

likelihood

ratios

(Altman

&

Bland,

1994;

Grimes

&

Schulz,

2005)

for

each

domain-diagnosis

pair.


Sensitivities

and

specificities

higher

than

0.75

(Power

et

al.,

2013),

LR+

values

higher

than

2

and

LR-

values

lower

than

0.5

were

considered

clinically

useful

(Grimes

&

Schulz,

2005;

Jaeschke,

Guyatt,

&

Sackett,

1994).

Exact

binomial

95%

confidence

intervals

(95%

CI)

were

for

sensitivity

and

specificity

(Collett,

2002).

Confidence

intervals

for

LR+

and

LR-

values

are

based

on

formulae

by

Simel,

Samsa

&

Matchar

(1991).

Analysis

of

variability

in

screening

properties

by

framing

We

have

first

described

the

by-item

response

differences

and

calculated

the

polychoric

correlation

and

Cohen’s

kappa

to

measure

the

reliability

between

frames

for

each

DSM-XC

item.

Second,

we

calculated

and

compared

all

screening

properties

between

framings.

Overlapping

confidence

intervals

were

considered

statistically

equivalent.

Paired

Wilcoxon

tests

with

DSM-XC

domains

as

dependent

variables

were

conducted

to

compare

the

differences

in

screening

properties

between

the

two

framings.

Screening

properties

of

the

two

framings

were

also

compared

with

the

OR

rule

(reference

group)

with

paired

Wilcoxon

tests

with

DSM-XC

domains

as

dependent

variables.

Logistic

regression

models

were

used

to

test

potential

interactions

between

intensity

and

frequency

that

could

indicate

an

advantage

of

a

particular

framing.

The

odds

ratios

for

specific

combinations,

namely

Intensity

(-)

/

Frequency

(+),

Intensity

(+)

/

Frequency

(-)

and

Intensity

(+)

/

Frequency

(+)

were

calculated

with

Intensity

(-)

/

Frequency

(-)

as

the

reference

group

for

each

domain

with

a

corresponding

disorder.

We

also

tested

if

clinical

impairment

could

be

a

factor

for

potential

differences

in

framings

instead

of

the

framing

effect

itself.

Because

of

this,

secondary

analyses

were

conducted

by

removing

the

clinical

impairment

criteria.

The

diagnosis

of

AUD

was

based

on

AUDIT

scores

and

was

not

included

in

this

analysis.

All

were

software

R,

4.1.3.

2.0.44

(Stevenson

2022).

Wilcoxon

Discussion

This

is

the

first

study

to

describe

the

screening

properties

of

the

DSM-XC

for

a

broad

spectrum

of

psychiatric

diagnoses

in

a

large

community

sample.

Results

suggest

that

screening

for

psychiatric

conditions

using

simple

and

objective

operational

criteria

increases

the

likelihood

of

detection

or

may

help

to

rule

out

specific

diagnoses.

The

results

comprise

three

main

findings:

First,

the

DSM-XC

domains

are

not

diagnostic-specific,

rather,

they

function

as

transdiagnostic

screening

tools.

For

example,

a

negative

anxiety

domain

is

useful

in

decreasing

and

a

positive

suicidal

ideation

domain

is

useful

in

increasing

the

probability

of

many

internalizing

disorders.

Second,

the

screening

utility

of

the

DSM-XC

is

lower

for

externalizing

disorders.

Third,

“intensity”

and

“frequency”

framings

as

measured

by

the

DSM-XC

are

only

moderately

correlated,

and

the

“frequency”

framing

exhibited

a

lower

number

of

above-threshold

domains

and

improved

screening

properties

compared

to

“intensity”

framing.

While

several

screening

tools

exist

for

specific

diagnosis,

few

address

multiple

diagnostic

categories

simultaneously.

Despite

limitations

in

externalizing

disorder

assessment,

for

example

due

to

the

lack

of

ADHD

domain

in

the

DSM-XC

and

the

lack

of

a

diagnostic

interview

for

AUD

in

the

present

cohort,

the

DSM-XC

performance

for

depression

and

anxiety

is

comparable

to

existing

scales,

justifying

its

potential

applicability

in

community

settings.

The

Patient

Health

Questionnaire-2

(PHQ-2)

(Kroenke,

Spitzer

&

Williams,

2003)

assesses

similar

symptoms

to

the

depression

domain

of

the

DSM-XC,

querying

low

mood

and

loss

of

interest

over

the

past

2

weeks,

despite

differences

in

instructions

and

scoring

scales.

In

the

present

study,

we

found

screening

properties

of

the

DSM-XC

“OR”

rule

depression

domain

to

detect

MDD

(LR+

=

2.32,

LR-

=

0.08,

sensitivity

=

0.95,

specificity

=

0.59)

to

be

similar

to

recent

meta-analytic

evidence

examining

the

PHQ-2

(LR+

=

2.97,

LR-

=

0.26,

sensitivity

=

0.89,

specificity

=

0.75)

(Mitchell

et

al.,

2016).

The

Generalized

Anxiety

Disorder

two

questions

scale

(GAD-2)

with

a

cut-off

of

3

presents

more

informative

properties

(LR+

=

4.31,

LR-

=

0.25,

sensitivity

=

0.80,

specificity

=

0.81)

(Plummer

et

al.,

2016)

compared

to

the

DSM-XC

anxiety

domain

to

detect

GAD

(original

“OR”

rule

LR+

1.90,

LR-

=

0.24,

sensitivity

=

0.87,

specificity

=

0.54).

The

differences

in

performance

between

legacy

measures

with

similar

conceptual

content

and

DSM-XC

domains

may

be

attributed

to

variations

in

item

content,

scale

and

scoring

methods

(linear

vs.

algorithm).

For

instance,

the

DSM-XC

anxiety

domain

comprises

3

items,

includes

more

symptoms

per

item

and

assesses

different

symptoms,

such

as

panic

and

anxious

avoidance,

while

the

GAD-2

has

only

2

items

focusing

on

anxiety

and

worrying.

Additionally,

both

PHQ-2

and

GAD-2

use

4-point

scales,

while

the

DSM-XC

is

rated

on

a

5-point

scale.

A

lack

of

direct

correspondence

was

observed

across

domains

and

psychiatric

diagnoses.

Moreover,

some

domains

have

a

higher

capability

than

others

for

screening,

and

some

domains

showed

utility

in

screening

for

multiple

disorders

(transdiagnostic

utility).

For

example,

the

depression

domain

showed

a

LR+

of

2.32

for

detecting

MDD,

2.11

for

detecting

GAD,

and

1.94

for

PTSD.

Conversely,

the

anxiety

domain

showed

significant

LR-

values

for

all

internalizing

disorders,

suggesting

its

potential

as

a

first

screening

step.

This

finding

contrasts

with

the

current

understanding

of

the

DSM-XC

process

of

further

inquiring

an

individual

with

disorder-specific

questions

if

they

screen

positive

in

a

domain.

However,

the

DSM-XC

did

not

show

meaningful

utility

for

externalizing

disorders,

except

for

a

good

likelihood

ratio

of

a

negative

screen

in

the

substance

use

domain

to

rule

out

AUD.

Due

to

identified

shortcomings,

specific

recommended

scales

for

alcohol

and

substance

use

should

supplement

primary

care

assessments

using

the

DSM-XC.

Further

modifications

in

the

tool

are

necessary

to

address

externalizing

symptoms,

such

as

impulsivity

and

disruptive

behaviors,

aiming

at

increasing

overall

screening

utility.

These

targeted

improvements

could

broaden

the

DSM-XC's

scope

and

solidify

its

place

as

a

component

of

community

screening

strategies.

Strong

connections

observed

in

certain

domains'

screening

capabilities

likely

reflect

the

interconnectedness

of

the

disorders

they

captured.

The

presence

of

clinical

features

that

are

not

represented

in

the

diagnostic

criteria

but

are

frequent

among

individuals

with

certain

mental

disorders

is

a

potential

explanation

for

some

domains

demonstrating

screening

utility

for

multiple

disorders.

For

instance,

somatic

symptoms,

while

not

part

of

diagnostic

criteria,

may

be

more

commonly

experienced

among

individuals

with

GAD

and

MDD,

while

anxious

distress

is

a

notable

feature

in

both

bipolar

and

major

depressive

disorders

(Bartoli

et

al.,

2023).

Another

contributing

factor

is

the

conceptual

similarity

and

symptom

overlap

across

various

diagnostic

criteria,

with

insomnia

and

irritable

mood

being

among

the

top

non-specific

symptoms

(Forbes

et

al.,

2023).

In

our

study,

sleep

problems

and

anger,

for

example,

demonstrated

significant

positive

likelihood

ratios

across

anxiety,

mood,

and

post-traumatic

stress

disorder

categories.

Comorbidity

and

common

temperamental

risk

factors

can

contribute

to

this

phenomenon,

as

individuals

with

high

levels

of

negative

affectivity

(neuroticism)

are

likely

to

endorse

multiple

internalizing

symptom

domains

in

a

non-specific

manner

due

to

being

oriented

towards

negative

affectivity

(Griffith

et

al.,

2010).

Additionally,

substantial

evidence

supports

the

idea

that

common

neural

and

genetic

mechanisms

contribute

to

the

association

between

these

disorders

(Xie

et

al.,

2023,

Jami

et

al.,

2022).

We

also

examined

the

contributions

of

framing

questions

as

intensity

or

frequency

of

symptoms,

as

the

questionnaire

was

revised

based

on

participant

feedback

regarding

the

challenge

in

understanding

double-barrelled

questions.

The

DSM-XC

showed

moderate

correlation

between

framings,

with

intensity-framed

questions

leading

to

a

significantly

higher

proportion

of

positive

screens

for

most

domains

compared

to

frequency-framed

questions.

For

some

domains,

such

as

depression,

anger,

and

memory,

framing

questions

as

“intensity”

approximately

doubled

the

number

of

individuals

that

would

have

been

needed

to

complete

Level

2

Measures,

compared

with

“frequency”.

Thus,

using

frequency-framed

questions

may

be

a

more

resource-efficient

approach.


Framings

also

differed

in

screening

properties,

with

frequency-framed

questions

presenting

generally

higher

specificity

but

equivalent

sensitivity

to

detect

their

correspondent

specific

disorders.

Differences

in

LR+

favouring

the

use

of

the

“frequency”

framing

were

found,

with

minimal

compromise

in

LR-

values.

The

value

of

likelihood

ratios

for

clinical

decision

making

is

significant

(Grimes

&

Schulz,

2005).

For

example,

a

positive

result

in

the

anxiety

domain,

with

a

likelihood

ratio

of

1.95,

translates

to

a

shift

from

the

pre-test

probability

of

GAD

from

10.5%

to

a

post-test

probability

of

18.3%.

However,

by

employing

the

“frequency”

framing,

with

a

LR+

value

of

3.11,

the

post-test

probability

substantially

increases

to

26.8%

for

GAD.

As

the

conversion

from

pre-test

to

post-test

probability

involves

a

transformation

into

odds,

we

have

developed

an

accessible

tool,

available

at

https://pacheco-jpg.shinyapps.io/dsm_xc_shiny_app/

that

enables

quick

estimation

of

the

shift

from

pre-

to

post-test

probability

for

the

tested

disorders

within

the

DSM-XC

domains.

Apart

from

establishing

improved

screening

utility

for

the

DSM-XC,

defining

standards

for

adverbial

framing

of

questions

can

reduce

the

substantial

heterogeneity

in

mental

health

assessment

(Newson,

Hunter,

&

Thiagarajan,

2020).

Previous

work

suggests

higher

reliability,

criterion

validity

(Krishnakumar

et

al.,

2021)

and

stability

over

time

(Krabbe

&

Forkmann,

2014)

for

frequency

in

comparison

to

intensity,

which

could

explain

the

higher

accuracy

of

the

frequency

framing

that

we

found

in

the

present

study.

This

study

has

three

main

strengths.

First,

we

examined

a

community-based

sample,

which

allows

for

real-world

estimates

of

the

screening

properties

of

the

DSM-XC.

Second,

we

investigated

a

broad

spectrum

of

psychiatric

diagnoses,

with

examples

of

both

internalizing

and

externalizing

disorders.

Third,

we

removed

a

previous

restriction

imposed

by

double-barrelled

phrasing,

which

allowed

for

examining

the

contributions

of

intensity

and

frequency

framings.

However,

interpreting

these

results

requires

considering

several

limitations.

First,

results

should

not

be

necessarily

extrapolated

for

other

age

groups

as

the

sample

was

limited

to

the

age

of

22.

Second,

although

the

presence

of

most

disorders

was

determined

by

a

qualified

clinical

psychologist

with

a

structured

interview,

we

used

the

AUDIT

to

evaluate

AUD.

Third,

further

research

is

needed

to

directly

compare

the

implemented

“OR”

rule

with

the

original

double-barrelled

scale.

The

“OR”

rule

allowed

to

characterize

the

intended

meaning

of

the

DSM-XC,

which

is

an

important

as

it

addresses

the

cognitively

demanding

phrasing

of

the

original

scale.

A

notable

concern

with

the

implemented

approach

is

that

the

order

that

questions

were

presented

could

have

affected

how

individuals

rated

each

item.

As

the

“intensity”

framing

was

always

presented

first,

this

piece

of

information

could

have

influenced

how

participants

answered

the

following

“frequency”

question,

introducing

anchoring

bias.

However,

anchoring

bias

tends

to

make

results

look

more

similar

and

we

found

only

moderate

correlations

between

framings.

Additionally,

the

frequency

framing,

presented

after

intensity,

showed

better

screening

properties,

and

logistic

regression

analyses

of

specific

framing

subgroups

suggests

the

frequency

framing

captures

relevant

information

of

specific

corresponding

disorders

on

more

occasions

than

the

intensity

framing

alone.

This

suggests

that

anchoring

bias

did

not

occur

as

frequency

framing

is

not

conditioned

to

intensity

framing.

The

present

results

demonstrated

that

the

DSM-XC

is

useful

in

screening

multiple

domains

of

psychopathology,

increasing

or

decreasing

the

likelihood

of

detection

of

specific

diagnoses

with

simple

objective

questions.

Due

to

the

low

direct

correspondence

between

domain

and

diagnosis,

more

than

one

Level

2

Cross-Cutting

Symptom

Measures

could

apply

after

a

positive

screening

in

some

domains.

We

also

found

that

adverbial

framings

have

an

impact

on

the

DSM-XC’s

screening

performance.

Framing

questions

as

“frequency”

may

be

more

resource-efficient

and

could

lead

to

improved

detection

of

positive

cases.

We

recommend

that

these

findings

should

be

replicated

in

other

samples

to

allow

implementation

in

routine

practice

and

that

future

examination

of

scoring

thresholds

should

be

done

to

further

optimize

the

DSM-XC

as

a

screening

tool

for

mental

health

conditions.
