The

differences

in

performance

between

legacy

measures

with

similar

conceptual

content

and

DSM-XC

domains

may

be

attributed

to

variations

in

item

content,

scale

and

scoring

methods

(linear

vs.

algorithm).

For

instance,

the

DSM-XC

anxiety

domain

comprises

3

items,

includes

more

symptoms

per

item

and

assesses

different

symptoms,

such

as

panic

and

anxious

avoidance,

while

the

GAD-2

has

only

2

items

focusing

on

anxiety

and

worrying.

Additionally,

both

PHQ-2

and

GAD-2

use

4-point

scales,

while

the

DSM-XC

is

rated

on

a

5-point

scale.

A

lack

of

direct

correspondence

was

observed

across

domains

and

psychiatric

diagnoses.

Moreover,

some

domains

have

a

higher

capability

than

others

for

screening,

and

some

domains

showed

utility

in

screening

for

multiple

disorders

(transdiagnostic

utility).

For

example,

the

depression

domain

showed

a

LR+

of

2.32

for

detecting

MDD,

2.11

for

detecting

GAD,

and

1.94

for

PTSD.

Conversely,

the

anxiety

domain

showed

significant

LR-

values

for

all

internalizing

disorders,

suggesting

its

potential

as

a

first

screening

step.

This

finding

contrasts

with

the

current

understanding

of

the

DSM-XC

process

of

further

inquiring

an

individual

with

disorder-specific

questions

if

they

screen

positive

in

a

domain.

However,

the

DSM-XC

did

not

show

meaningful

utility

for

externalizing

disorders,

except

for

a

good

likelihood

ratio

of

a

negative

screen

in

the

substance

use

domain

to

rule

out

AUD.

Due

to

identified

shortcomings,

specific

recommended

scales

for

alcohol

and

substance

use

should

supplement

primary

care

assessments

using

the

DSM-XC.

Further

modifications

in

the

tool

are

necessary

to

address

externalizing

symptoms,

such

as

impulsivity

and

disruptive

behaviors,

aiming

at

increasing

overall

screening

utility.

These

targeted

improvements

could

broaden

the

DSM-XC's

scope

and

solidify

its

place

as

a

component

of

community

screening

strategies.

Strong

connections

observed

in

certain

domains'

screening

capabilities

likely

reflect

the

interconnectedness

of

the

disorders

they

captured.

The

presence

of

clinical

features

that

are

not

represented

in

the

diagnostic

criteria

but

are

frequent

among

individuals

with

certain

mental

disorders

is

a

potential

explanation

for

some

domains

demonstrating

screening

utility

for

multiple

disorders.

For

instance,

somatic

symptoms,

while

not

part

of

diagnostic

criteria,

may

be

more

commonly

experienced

among

individuals

with

GAD

and

MDD,

while

anxious

distress

is

a

notable

feature

in

both

bipolar

and

major

depressive

disorders

(Bartoli

et

al.,

2023).

Another

contributing

factor

is

the

conceptual

similarity

and

symptom

overlap

across

various

diagnostic

criteria,

with

insomnia

and

irritable

mood

being

among

the

top

non-specific

symptoms

(Forbes

et

al.,

2023).

In

our

study,

sleep

problems

and

anger,

for

example,

demonstrated

significant

positive

likelihood

ratios

across

anxiety,

mood,

and

post-traumatic

stress

disorder

categories.

Comorbidity

and

common

temperamental

risk

factors

can

contribute

to

this

phenomenon,

as

individuals

with

high

levels

of

negative

affectivity

(neuroticism)

are

likely

to

endorse

multiple

internalizing

symptom

domains

in

a

non-specific

manner

due

to

being

oriented

towards

negative

affectivity

(Griffith

et

al.,

2010).

Additionally,

substantial

evidence

supports

the

idea

that

common

neural

and

genetic

mechanisms

contribute

to

the

association

between

these

disorders

(Xie

et

al.,

2023,

Jami

et

al.,

2022).

We

also

examined

the

contributions

of

framing

questions

as

intensity

or

frequency

of

symptoms,

as

the

questionnaire

was

revised

based

on

participant

feedback

regarding

the

challenge

in

understanding

double-barrelled

questions.

The

DSM-XC

showed

moderate

correlation

between

framings,

with

intensity-framed

questions

leading

to

a

significantly

higher

proportion

of

positive

screens

for

most

domains

compared

to

frequency-framed

questions.

For

some

domains,

such

as

depression,

anger,

and

memory,

framing

questions

as

“intensity”

approximately

doubled

the

number

of

individuals

that

would

have

been

needed

to

complete

Level

2

Measures,

compared

with

“frequency”.

Thus,

using

frequency-framed

questions

may

be

a

more

resource-efficient

approach.


Framings

also

differed

in

screening

properties,

with

frequency-framed

questions

presenting

generally

higher

specificity

but

equivalent

sensitivity

to

detect

their

correspondent

specific

disorders.

Differences

in

LR+

favouring

the

use

of

the

“frequency”

framing

were

found,

with

minimal

compromise

in

LR-

values.

The

value

of

likelihood

ratios

for

clinical

decision

making

is

significant

(Grimes

&

Schulz,

2005).

For

example,

a

positive

result

in

the

anxiety

domain,

with

a

likelihood

ratio

of

1.95,

translates

to

a

shift

from

the

pre-test

probability

of

GAD

from

10.5%

to

a

post-test

probability

of

18.3%.

However,

by

employing

the

“frequency”

framing,

with

a

LR+

value

of

3.11,

the

post-test

probability

substantially

increases

to

26.8%

for

GAD.

As

the

conversion

from

pre-test

to

post-test

probability

involves

a

transformation

into

odds,

we

have

developed

an

accessible

tool,

available

at

https://pacheco-jpg.shinyapps.io/dsm_xc_shiny_app/

that

enables

quick

estimation

of

the

shift

from

pre-

to

post-test

probability

for

the

tested

disorders

within

the

DSM-XC

domains.

Apart

from

establishing

improved

screening

utility

for

the

DSM-XC,

defining

standards

for

adverbial

framing

of

questions

can

reduce

the

substantial

heterogeneity

in

mental

health

assessment

(Newson,

Hunter,

&

Thiagarajan,

2020).

Previous

work

suggests

higher

reliability,

criterion

validity

(Krishnakumar

et

al.,

2021)

and

stability

over

time

(Krabbe

&

Forkmann,

2014)

for

frequency

in

comparison

to

intensity,

which

could

explain

the

higher

accuracy

of

the

frequency

framing

that

we

found

in

the

present

study.

This

study

has

three

main

strengths.

First,

we

examined

a

community-based

sample,

which

allows

for

real-world

estimates

of

the

screening

properties

of

the

DSM-XC.

Second,

we

investigated

a

broad

spectrum

of

psychiatric

diagnoses,

with

examples

of

both

internalizing

and

externalizing

disorders.

Third,

we

removed

a

previous

restriction

imposed

by

double-barrelled

phrasing,

which

allowed

for

examining

the

contributions

of

intensity

and

frequency

framings.

However,

interpreting

these

results

requires

considering

several

limitations.

First,

results

should

not

be

necessarily

extrapolated

for

other

age

groups

as

the

sample

was

limited

to

the

age

of

22.

Second,

although

the

presence

of

most

disorders

was

determined

by

a

qualified

clinical

psychologist

with

a

structured

interview,

we

used

the

AUDIT

to

evaluate

AUD.

Third,

further

research

is

needed

to

directly

compare

the

implemented

“OR”

rule

with

the

original

double-barrelled

scale.

The

“OR”

rule

allowed

to

characterize

the

intended

meaning

of

the

DSM-XC,

which

is

an

important

as

it

addresses

the

cognitively

demanding

phrasing

of

the

original

scale.

A

notable

concern

with

the

implemented

approach

is

that

the

order

that

questions

were

presented

could

have

affected

how

individuals

rated

each

item.

As

the

“intensity”

framing

was

always

presented

first,

this

piece

of

information

could

have

influenced

how

participants

answered

the

following

“frequency”

question,

introducing

anchoring

bias.

However,

anchoring

bias

tends

to

make

results

look

more

similar

and

we

found

only

moderate

correlations

between

framings.

Additionally,

the

frequency

framing,

presented

after

intensity,

showed

better

screening

properties,

and

logistic

regression

analyses

of

specific

framing

subgroups

suggests

the

frequency

framing

captures

relevant

information

of

specific

corresponding

disorders

on

more

occasions

than

the

intensity

framing

alone.

This

suggests

that

anchoring

bias

did

not

occur

as

frequency

framing

is

not

conditioned

to

intensity

framing.

The

present

results

demonstrated

that

the

DSM-XC

is

useful

in

screening

multiple

domains

of

psychopathology,

increasing

or

decreasing

the

likelihood

of

detection

of

specific

diagnoses

with

simple

objective

questions.

Due

to

the

low

direct

correspondence

between

domain

and

diagnosis,

more

than

one

Level

2

Cross-Cutting

Symptom

Measures

could

apply

after

a

positive

screening

in

some

domains.

We

also

found

that

adverbial

framings

have

an

impact

on

the

DSM-XC’s

screening

performance.

Framing

questions

as

“frequency”

may

be

more

resource-efficient

and

could

lead

to

improved

detection

of

positive

cases.

We

recommend

that

these

findings

should

be

replicated

in

other

samples

to

allow

implementation

in

routine

practice

and

that

future

examination

of

scoring

thresholds

should

be

done

to

further

optimize

the

DSM-XC

as

a

screening

tool

for

mental

health

conditions.

FINAL

REMARKS

The

research

presented

in

this

thesis

evaluated

the

DSM-XC

for

the

detection,

comorbidity

assessment,

and

clinical

staging

of

mental

disorders

in

a

community-based

sample

of

youth.

By

addressing

critical

gaps

in

the

literature,

these

three

studies

provide

empirical

evidence

to

support

a

shift

from

single-disorder

screening

toward

a

transdiagnostic,

stage-based

framework

for

youth

mental

health.

4.1

Synthesis

of

main

findings

Collectively,

the

findings

challenge

the

traditional

disorder-specific

paradigm

of

mental

health

screening.

The

first

study

demonstrated

that

DSM-XC

domains

function

as

transdiagnostic

indicators

rather

than

disorder-specific

measures,

with

individual

domains

consistently

influencing

the

probability

of

multiple

internalizing

disorders

simultaneously.

Furthermore,

a

comparison

revealed

that

framing

questions

based

on

“frequency”

(“how

often”)

yields

superior

diagnostic

accuracy,

in

particular

higher

specificity

and

positive

likelihood

ratios,

compared

to

“intensity”

(“how

much”),

without

compromising

sensitivity.

Although

the

DSM-XC

was

designed

as

a

multidimensional

screening

tool,

the

present

results

indicate

that

its

structure

is

heavily

oriented

toward

internalizing

symptomatology.

These

symptoms

frequently

aggregate

into

highly

comorbid

diagnostic

groupings

(De

Vries

et

al.

2022)

that

may

reflect

a

common

underlying

liability

(Caspi

et

al.

2025;

Caspi

et

al.

2020;

McGrath

et

al.

2020;

Plana-Ripoll

et

al.

2019),

supported

by

partially

overlapping

genetic

(Bourque

et

al.

2024),

neurobiological

(Xie

et

al.

2023),

and

treatment-response

profiles

(Barlow

et

al.

2020;

Cuijpers

et

al.

2023;

Gosmann

et

al.

2021;

Leichsenring

et

al.

2022).

Consequently,

internalizing

categories

may

exhibit

limited

diagnostic

distinctiveness,

which

constrains

their

utility

for

screening,

despite

capturing

phenomenologically

distinct

experiences

(e.g.,

anhedonia

versus

acute

anxiety).

While

some

degree

of

shared

variance

is

expected

within

transdiagnostic

frameworks

(Simms

et

al.

2023),

multidimensional

tools

would

likely

benefit

from

improved

differentiation

across

domains

to

reduce

excessive

interdependence.

In

this

context,

broader

representation

of

externalizing

and

thought-related

symptoms

may

enhance

the

balance

of

the

DSM-XC.

More

comprehensive

dimensional

assessment

may

also

require

the

inclusion

of

additional

parameters,

such

as

symptom

persistence

and

global

functioning

(Correll

et

al.

2025),

which

are

central

to

clinical

staging

(Scott

et

al.

2024)

and

risk

stratification

but

are

not

directly

captured

by

the

current

measure.

The

second

study

further

clarified

the

performance

of

the

DSM-XC

in

the

context

of

psychiatric

comorbidity.

Thresholds

originally

proposed

for

the

DSM-5

(
i.e.
,

domain

scores

≥2

for

anxiety,

depression,

and

mania

domains,

and

≥1

for

substance

use)

showed

utility

for

excluding

additional

diagnoses,

as

indicated

by

high

sensitivity

and

negative

predictive

value.

However,

they

were

less

effective

for

confirming

these

diagnoses

due

to

limited

specificity.

Increasing

domain-level

cut-offs

resulted

in

modest

improvements

in

the

identification

of

comorbid

conditions,

particularly

for

depressive,

anxiety,

and

substance

use

disorders,

yielding

positive

likelihood

ratios

in

the

range

of

approximately

2.0.

However,

this

magnitude

of

likelihood

ratio

corresponds

to

only

a

small

shift

in

post-test

diagnostic

probability,

indicating

that

domain

scores

alone

remain

insufficient

for

confidently

ruling

in

comorbid

diagnoses,

even

under

optimized

thresholds.

Accordingly,

the

DSM-XC

appears

more

appropriately

positioned

as

a

triage

tool

to

inform

the

need

for

more

detailed

diagnostic

evaluation,

rather

than

as

a

substitute

for

it.

In

practical

terms,

a

positive

domain

score

should

not

be

interpreted

as

confirming

the

presence

of

a

specific

comorbid

condition,

but

rather

as

an

indication

that

systematic

clinical

assessment

for

additional

disorders

is

warranted.

For

example,

in

individuals

presenting

with

a

high

pre-test

probability

of

psychopathology

in

routine

clinical

care,

elevated

DSM-XC

scores

would

support

the

need

to

investigate

a

broader

range

of

potential

comorbidities

beyond

the

chief

complaint,

irrespective

of

which

specific

domain

thresholds

are

met.

In

contrast,

aggregate

scoring

approaches

may

offer

a

pragmatic

means

of

identifying

individuals

with

elevated

overall

symptom

burden

and

increased

likelihood

of

diagnostic

complexity.

In

other

words,

combining

domain-level

screening

(to

support

exclusion)

with

total

score–based

indicators

(to

flag

clinical

complexity)

may

improve

the

timely

recognition

of

individuals

requiring

more

comprehensive

assessment.

Finally,

the

third

study

assessed

the

application

of

a

transdiagnostic

clinical

staging

framework

in

the

community.

The

DSM-XC

captured

coherent

cross-cutting

symptom

profiles

across

mood,

anxiety,

and

post-traumatic

stress

disorders,

mirroring

a

potentially

unifiable

transdiagnostic

construct.

Stages

reflected

a

continuum

of

affective

and

stress-related

dysregulation

across

these

conditions

and

were

associated

with

graded

increases

in

objective

burden,

including

cardiometabolic

risk,

maladaptive

health

behaviours,

suicidality,

and

educational

and

occupational

disadvantage.

These

stages

corresponded

to

distinct

gradients

of

burden:

cardiometabolic

and

behavioural

risks

emerged

in

early

and

subthreshold

stages

(Stage

1b),

whereas

suicidality

and

severe

socioeconomic

disadvantage

were

heavily

concentrated

in

persistent

or

recurrent

stages

(Stage

3+).

Staging

trajectories

converged

along

a

shared

dimension

of

symptom

severity

and

functional

impairment,

indicating

comparable

clinical

burden

across

diagnostic

categories

at

similar

stages.

Consistent

with

life-course

evidence

(Caspi

et

al.

2020;

Clarke

et

al.

2025;

McGrath

et

al.

2020;

Plana-Ripoll

et

al.

2019),

later

stages

were

marked

by

greater

comorbidity

and

clinical

complexity.

4.2

Implications

for

clinical

assessment

and

public

health

These

findings

have

direct

implications

for

clinical

practice

and

public

health

planning:

1.

Standardization

of

assessment:

The

superior

performance

of

frequency-based

framing

indicates

that

future

iterations

of

the

DSM-XC

and

comparable

screening

tools

should

prioritize

“how

often”

phrasing

to

improve

diagnostic

precision,

possibly

by

reducing

cognitive

burden,

and

enhancing

resource

efficiency.

Standardization

of

adverbial

framing

may

also

reduce

heterogeneity

across

assessment

measures

and

improve

comparability

across

clinical

and

epidemiological

settings.

2.

Implications

for

multidimensional

measurement:

Although

the

DSM-XC

is

explicitly

conceived

as

a

multidimensional

assessment

tool,

its

symptom

content

appears

disproportionately

weighted

toward

internalizing

domains.

This

imbalance

likely

reflects

the

strong

empirical

coherence

of

internalizing

symptoms

but

may

also

limit

the

tool’s

capacity

to

distinguish

between

partially

overlapping

conditions

that

share

common

latent,

genetic,

and

neurobiological

substrates.

Consequently,

several

DSM-XC

domains

may

function

more

as

indicators

of

shared

internalizing

liability

than

as

discrete

dimensions

with

independent

heuristic

value.

A

more

balanced

multidimensional

measure

would

benefit

from

greater

representation

of

externalizing

and

thought-related

symptoms,

as

well

as

clearer

separation

between

dimensions,

to

avoid

excessive

overlap

while

preserving

the

advantages

of

transdiagnostic

assessment.

As

it

stands,

any

above

threshold

endorsement

of

a

DSM-XC

domain

mandates

screening

for

several

disorders,

not

only

the

one

intended

by

the

domain.

3.

Refining

comorbidity

screening:

Although

the

DSM-XC

is

intended

to

facilitate

the

detection

of

comorbidity,

its

predominantly

internalizing

structure

has

implications

for

how

results

should

be

interpreted

in

clinical

practice.

In

settings

where

a

primary

diagnosis

has

already

been

established,

the

use

of

lower

DSM-XC

thresholds

may

be

efficient

for

ruling

out

additional

conditions.

However,

when

the

objective

is

to

identify

and

confirm

comorbid

disorders,

a

common

requirement

in

youth

mental

health

care,

higher

thresholds

may

be

necessary,

albeit

with

limited

rule-in

capacity.

In

this

context,

the

DSM-XC

total

score

may

serve

as

a

pragmatic

screener

for

the

broader

symptom

burden

associated

with

psychiatric

comorbidity.

In

time-constrained

clinical

environments,

a

total

score

of

21

or

higher

could

function

as

an

alert

to

a

potentially

multimorbid

clinical

presentation,

prompting

a

comprehensive

diagnostic

evaluation

regardless

of

the

presenting

complaint.

4.

Stage-informed

framework

for

community

mental

health

assessment:

The

observed

alignment

between

DSM-XC

symptom

profiles

and

transdiagnostic

clinical

stages

raises

the

possibility

that

the

tool

could

assist

in

identifying

stage-related

gradients

of

clinical

burden

in

community

settings.

In

this

context,

DSM-XC–derived

symptom

patterns

may

help

inform

preliminary

stratification

according

to

overall

symptom

severity

and

functional

impact,

thereby

supporting

triage

decisions

within

stepped-care

models.

However,

the

extent

to

which

brief

multidimensional

screeners

can

be

used

to

operationalize

staging-informed

allocation

of

care

has

not

yet

been

formally

evaluated

and

warrants

further

investigation.

Beyond

assessment

measure-level

considerations,

these

findings

also

support

the

broader

applicability

of

transdiagnostic

staging

frameworks

for

organizing

mental

health

needs

at

the

population

level.

In

resource-constrained

settings,

such

as

many

LMICs,

a

stage-informed

approach

may

facilitate

more

proportionate

allocation

of

services

across

community,

primary,

and

specialized

care

by

targeting

intervention

intensity

according

to

level

of

clinical

burden

rather

than

discrete

diagnostic

categories

alone

(Buchweitz

et

al.

2026).

From

a

public

health

perspective,

this

may

represent

a

scalable

hypothesis

for

service

planning

in

contexts

characterized

by

high

prevalence

of

internalizing

symptoms

and

limited

access

to

specialist

assessment,

to

be

tested

in

future

implementation-focused

research.

4.3

Methodological

considerations

and

limitations

While

this

thesis

draws

on

a

large,

population-based

birth

cohort

and

structured

diagnostic

interviews,

several

overarching

methodological

limitations

should

be

acknowledged.

First,

all

analyses

were

conducted

using

cross-sectional

data

collected

at

age

22,

which

precludes

conclusions

regarding

the

temporal

stability

of

symptom

patterns

or

measurement

properties

across

developmental

periods.

Accordingly,

the

performance

of

the

DSM-XC,

including

domain-level

associations

and

optimal

thresholds,

may

vary

over

time

or

across

stages

of

illness.

Second,

the

sample

was

restricted

to

a

single

birth

cohort

from

Southern

Brazil,

which

may

limit

the

generalizability

of

findings

to

other

age

groups,

cultural

contexts,

or

healthcare

systems.

Differences

in

help-seeking

behavior,

service

availability,

or

symptom

expression

across

settings

may

influence

both

tool

performance

and

the

applicability

of

derived

thresholds

or

symptom

profiles.

Finally,

the

set

of

disorders

assessed

with

structured

diagnostic

interviews

was

restricted

to

selected

common

mental

disorders.

The

inclusion

of

additional

conditions,

such

as

substance

use

disorders

assessed

with

dedicated

structured

modules,

psychotic

disorders,

or

neurodevelopmental

syndromes,

could

provide

a

more

comprehensive

evaluation

of

DSM-XC

performance

across

a

broader

range

of

psychopathological

domains.

4.4

Future

research

directions

Future

research

is

required

to

evaluate

modifications

to

the

DSM-XC.

Additional

studies

should

test

the

clinical

impact

of

using

exclusively

frequency-based

questions,

as

well

as

alternative

clinical

thresholds

for

DSM-XC

domains

to

improve

the

identification

of

mental

disorders

in

community

samples.

In

parallel,

refinements

to

the

DSM-XC,

including

greater

representation

of

externalizing

and

thought-related

symptoms,

the

inclusion

of

metrics

capturing

chronicity

and

persistence,

and

the

suppression

of

redundant

or

closely

related

internalizing

items,

should

be

evaluated

to

determine

whether

they

enhance

its

performance

as

a

multidimensional

screening

tool.

Furthermore,

if

the

measure

remains

published

in

its

current

format,

an

alternative

diagnostic

pathway

should

be

formally

tested:

rather

than

using

DSM-XC

domains

to

trigger

disorder-specific

Level

2

assessments,

research

should

evaluate

whether

the

presence

of

any

positive

item

may

serve

as

an

indication

for

comprehensive

cross-domain

assessment.

Further

research

is

also

needed

to

examine

whether

DSM-XC–derived

symptom

profiles

can

meaningfully

contribute

to

stage-informed

allocation

of

care

within

youth

mental

health

services.

Beyond

these

considerations,

longitudinal

studies

are

required

to

determine

whether

DSM-XC–derived

symptom

patterns

prospectively

predict

stage

progression,

increasing

clinical

complexity,

or

functional

decline

over

time.

Tracking

individuals

across

developmental

periods

will

be

critical

to

establish

whether

specific

DSM-XC

domains

are

associated

with

transitions

from

nonspecific

or

subthreshold

presentations

to

persistent

and

impairing

illness.

In

addition,

empirical

studies

should

evaluate

whether

the

DSM-XC

total

score

is

capable

of

differentiating

between

adjacent

early

stages

(e.g.,

Stage

0

vs.

1a

or

Stage

1a

vs.

1b),

which

may

provide

clinically

relevant

information

for

early

risk

stratification.

Although

staging

frameworks

are

often

assumed

to

support

proportionate

care

by

matching

intervention

intensity

to

illness

severity,

this

premise

remains

largely

untested

in

community

samples.

In

particular,

the

assumption

that

individuals

in

more

advanced

stages

necessarily

require

more

invasive

or

resource-intensive

interventions

requires

direct

empirical

evaluation.

Future

implementation

studies

should

therefore

assess

whether

stage-informed

approaches

improve

the

allocation

of

limited

mental

health

resources

when

compared

to

conventional

disorder-based

screening

strategies

in

the

community.

4.5

Conclusion

This

thesis

provides

empirical

evidence

regarding

the

performance

of

the

DSM-XC

as

a

screening

tool

in

youth

community

settings.

Frequency-based

response

options

demonstrated

superior

diagnostic

performance

when

compared

to

intensity-based

scoring,

supporting

their

use

in

population-level

screening

contexts.

DSM-XC

domains

showed

transdiagnostic

associations

across

internalizing

disorders,

challenging

assumptions

of

disorder-specific

functioning

that

underpin

many

current

screening

practices,

as

well

as

the

assumption

that

the

tool

functions

multidimensionally.

These

findings

suggest

that

the

DSM-XC

may

be

better

suited

for

the

identification

of

internalizing

conditions

and

shared

symptom

burden

than

for

disorder-specific

case

detection.

Addressing

the

detection

of

co-occurring

mental

disorders

in

community

settings,

the

DSM-XC

demonstrated

utility

for

excluding

additional

diagnoses

when

original

domain

thresholds

were

applied

in

individuals

with

an

established

condition,

although

their

specificity

for

confirming

comorbid

disorders

was

limited.

Adjusting

these

thresholds

yielded

modest

gains

in

diagnostic

accuracy

across

internalizing

domains.

In

this

context,

the

DSM-XC

total

score

emerged

as

a

potential

indicator

of

cumulative

symptom

burden

associated

with

psychiatric

multimorbidity.

In

practice,

elevated

total

scores

may

serve

as

a

signal

of

increased

likelihood

of

co-occurring

conditions,

warranting

a

more

comprehensive

diagnostic

assessment

beyond

the

initially

identified

disorder.

The

transdiagnostic

clinical

staging

framework

appeared

to

capture

meaningful

gradients

of

burden

in

this

community

sample,

with

successive

stages

associated

with

progressive

increases

in

objective

indicators

such

as

cardiometabolic

risk,

maladaptive

health

behaviours,

suicidality,

and

educational

and

occupational

disadvantage.

These

findings

suggest

that

staging

models

may

be

applicable

for

structuring

population-level

mental

health

assessment

based

on

gradients

of

real-world

risk

and

impairment.

In

parallel,

cross-cutting

symptom

patterns

derived

from

the

DSM-XC

showed

systematic

variation

across

these

stages,

capturing

gradients

of

affective

and

stress-related

dysregulation

across

mood,

anxiety,

and

post-traumatic

stress

conditions.

This

correspondence

indicates

that

DSM-XC–based

symptom

profiles

may

be

used

to

characterize

stage-related

differences

in

clinical

presentation

and

could

contribute

to

stage-informed

approaches

to

assessment

and

service

planning.

Taken

together,

these

findings

support

the

use

of

brief

cross-cutting

measures

such

as

the

DSM-XC

as

tools

for

the

timely

identification

of

individuals

unlikely

to

meet

criteria

for

additional

mental

disorders

in

screening

contexts,

while

also

highlighting

the

broader

applicability

of

transdiagnostic

frameworks

for

structuring

mental

health

assessment

and

service

planning

among

young

people.

Moving

beyond

strictly

disorder-specific

screening

models

may

represent

an

important

step

toward

more

scalable

approaches

to

youth

mental

health

care

in

community

contexts.

Similarly,

moving

beyond

binary

present–absent

approaches

to

diagnosis

that

may

obscure

meaningful

gradients

of

symptom

burden

may

contribute

to

more

clinically

informative

assessment

strategies.
